title: Tulsidas bows to the whole world
hook: Tulsidas opens his Ramayana bowing to the saints, the wicked, and a world full of Sita and Ram
carry: the whole world is full of Sita and Ram
tomorrow: why does the Hanuman Chalisa start with a mirror?

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tulsidas bowed to Vani and Vinayaka at the door of the Ramcharitmanas, and wrote for his own heart's joy.

Speeches at a wedding usually go the same way. Thank the parents. Thank the friends who flew in. Thank the cooks. Tulsidas, at the door of his great poem, does something like that, but stranger. He bows to his teacher. He bows to the saints. And then, with what sounds like a straight face, he bows to the wicked, the people who wish others harm. He means it. And the reason he gives is the lesson.
screen: `HE BOWS TO THE TEACHER.` → `HE BOWS TO THE SAINTS.` → `THEN HE BOWS TO THE WICKED.`

segments.voice: The opening of the Ramcharitmanas is a long series of bows. First the teacher. Then the saints, and here Tulsidas has a lovely picture. He calls the company of good people a pilgrimage that walks: like Prayag, which the poem calls the king of pilgrimage places, but moving about the world on its own feet. It comes down your street. Then he bows to the wicked, sincerely, he says: people glad at another's loss and sad at another's gain. Why bow to them? He doesn't pretend they're good. Part of it is a poet's humility: he asks even the hostile reader to be kind to the poem. The deeper reason is a picture of the world. Tulsidas says the maker made this world a mixture, the living and the lifeless, good qualities and faults, all woven together. And the saint is like the swan in the old story, that can take the milk out of milk mixed with water, and leave the water behind. Good and bad come mixed, sometimes inside the same person. The work is to take the milk. Knowing the whole world to be full of Sita and Ram, Tulsidas says, he bows to it all with joined palms. That's the teaching, one of Hinduism's biggest: God isn't only in the temple. The whole world is full of Sita and Ram, so a devotee greets all of it with joined palms. Many Hindus explain namaste the same way: the palms meet because God is there in the other person too.
screen: `A PILGRIMAGE THAT WALKS.` · `A BOW TO THE WICKED.` · `THE SWAN TAKES THE MILK.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE WORLD FULL OF SITA AND RAM.`

segments.voice: Bring your palms together at your chest, or just rest your hands, and bring to mind three people: someone good to you, someone you hardly notice, someone you find difficult. For each, without changing your opinion, look for the milk in the mixture, one small good thing that's really there. Let a quiet bow go toward each of them, and if you pray, say Sita Ram softly for each, the greeting many Ram devotees use.
Tulsidas. The poet who bowed to the saints, the wicked, and a whole world full of Sita and Ram.
Your line: the whole world is full of Sita and Ram. The swan finds the milk, even in people who are hard to love. Tomorrow: why does the Hanuman Chalisa start with a mirror?

howItsDone: Readers of the Ramcharitmanas begin with its opening invocations, and the line about the whole world being full of Sita and Ram is often recited on its own with folded hands.

chat.says: nani's hosting bhajan night saturday and mr. kessler next door already complained about the noise. she did a full namaste to him anyway 😤 why bow to HIM??
options: Tulsidas bowed even to the wicked: the whole world is full of Sita and Ram, so nani greets God in him too.
it's just good manners. it doesn't mean anything religious.
nani's hoping the bow will make him stop complaining.
chat.meaning: Tulsidas bowed to the saints and to the wicked, because he saw the whole world full of Sita and Ram. Nani's namaste greets God in Mr. Kessler, not his complaint.

Prayag.meaning: a holy place where rivers meet, called king of pilgrimage places

Sita.meaning: Ram's wife, honored with him as divine

Ramcharitmanas.meaning: Tulsidas's retelling of Ram's story in Awadhi

Tulsidas.meaning: the poet of Ram who wrote the Ramcharitmanas

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm the order of the bows in Bal Kand (guru, saints, the wicked, then the world as Sita-Ram) and that it's fair to compress it this way.
'A pilgrimage that walks' paraphrases the line calling the company of saints a moving tirtharaj (Prayag); confirm.
The swan (hamsa) separating milk from water: confirm the Bal Kand doha on the world as a mixture of good and faults and the saint as the swan.
'He asks even the hostile reader to be kind to the poem' summarizes the khal vandana; confirm.
Original left null to avoid repeating yesterday's title word.
